newsitem.title: TAIWAN: INTERVIEW - Taiwan finance minister says stocks sound.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Taiwan finance minister says stocks sound.

text.p: Taiwan Finance Minister Paul Chiu said on Friday the island's rallying stock market was healthy and that a nightmarish crash in 1990 was unlikely to recur now.
"The economy is good and the stock market is quite sound," Chiu told Reuters Financial Television in an interview.

Taiwan's benchmark stock index has risen more than 40 percent since the beginning of 1997 and roughly doubled since rival Beijing test-fired missiles near the island in March 1996 in a bout of sabre-rattling that sparked a panicked exodus of funds from the stock market.
Many officials and analysts have raised concerns that Taiwan's market, which on July 31 surpassed the 10,000-point threshold for the first time since 1990, may be overheated.

Central bank governor Sheu Yuan-dong last week cited a "consensus" that the market may be slightly overheated with its recent torrential turnover, but said the bank had no opinion on whether the index was too high.
Chiu, however, said the market was "normal".
Unlike the economic bubble that burst seven years ago, today's Taiwan economy was well-sustained by strong fundamentals and the stock market was much "deeper and broader", Chiu said.
"In terms of market capitalisation and overall financial surrounding...it is very different," Chiu said.
The stock index crashed some 80 percent after hitting an all-time peak of 12,495.34 in 1990.
At that time, money supply was growing some 20-30 percent against less than 10 percent growth recently and the stock market's total value was only about a quarter of today's total, Chiu said.
Recent economic data supported Chiu's bullish view.
Taiwan's exports and imports soared to all-time peaks in July while the trade surplus narrowed 59.6 percent to US$543 million.
July exports totalled US$10.7 billion and imports were US$10.16 billion, both record highs for a single month.
"These are very strong figures and it indicates a very bustling economy," said Nomura Securities analyst Amy Huang.
The capitalist island posted gross domestic product growth of 6.83 percent in the first quarter and is on track to grow 6.24 percent for all of 1997, according to state projections.
Ting Kong Securities manager Tsao Chung-ping said the market shared Chiu's optimism.
"Most investors are optimistic about the stock market as well as the economy, so what Chiu said reflected general sentiment," Tsao said.
On Friday, the weighted index closed 82.96 points, or 0.84 percent, higher at 9,923.84.

Chiu said the stock market boom would help the government realise its ambition to turn the island into a regional financial centre and continue to liberalise and internationalise its financial markets.
The ministry would continue to encourage foreign institutions to issue bonds in Taiwan and promote direct listing of foreign companies in the island's stock market, he said.

The Asian Development Bank, the Central American Bank for Economic Integration, Nordic Investment Bank and European Bank for Reconstruction and Development all came to Taiwan to raise funds, Chiu said.
"We welcome this kind of issuing. We are now taking a further step to encourage foreign institutional investors or international financial organisations to issue bonds in Taiwan," Chiu said.

He nonetheless said the government had no immediate plans to completely ease a 25 percent foreign investment ceiling on Taiwan's stock market, but added the government was committed to free capital movement by 2000.
"We will drop the 25 percent ceiling when the market is well-developed," Chiu said.
